slides.title: 5 frozen pipe myths to drop before the first hard freeze

slides.myth: A pipe bursts right where the ice is.
slides.fact: It usually splits somewhere else. The ice plug traps water against a closed faucet, pressure builds there, and the pipe gives way where there's little or no ice.
slides.source: Live Science, This Old House, JLC

slides.myth: Frozen pipes are only a problem up north.
slides.fact: Southern homes can be more at risk. Pipes there often run through exterior walls and attics, because houses are built for heat, not hard freezes.

slides.myth: Letting a faucet drip just wastes water.
slides.fact: On frigid nights, even a trickle of cold water through the pipe helps keep it from freezing.

slides.myth: Turn the heat off while you're away for the holidays.
slides.fact: Leave it on, set no lower than 55°F, so the pipes inside your walls stay above freezing.

slides.myth: A torch is the fastest way to thaw a frozen pipe.
slides.fact: Never use an open flame. Keep the faucet open and use a hair dryer, a space heater or warm towels instead.
